en: When war broke out between the still and the restless
a clanging note rang in the hard chains,
then you came down, waterfall, in a rhythm that unbinds --
I know you, I know you.
In the song of union with the sea
you have risen wild to defy the rule of stone
in restless rhythm, O great rebel --
I know you, I know you.
O fearless one,
your anklets ringing with the self-forgetting beat of Rudra,
your feet striding through the gateway of death,
forever going forth to your tryst,
I know you.
From sky to sky she races, shouting --
Baishakhi the storm, lightning her word, thunder her army,
waking the rhythm of defiant speed in the branches of great trees.
Drunk on the wine of emptiness, the bird races on,
scattering the rhythm of the unseen road from wings of unbound speed.
Rhythm churns the depths of the heart
in the strife of white and black,
now in good, now in ill,
now straight, now crooked.
Rhythm danced in the waves of the sacrificial fire,
in the arched brow of the hero warring for freedom,
rhythm raced in the wheels of the terrible chariot on the road of doom.
Break -- break the dam, break the dam, break the dam.
Let captive life and mind fly free.
Into the dry riverbed let come
the wild sport of life's flood --
sing the victory-song of breaking.
Let the worn and old drift away,
drift away, drift away.
We have heard it -- fear not, fear not, fear not --
the call of something new.
We do not fear the unknown;
rush headlong at its barred door.
On wave after wave of that sea the trumpet has sounded, the trumpet has sounded.
When will my door swing open -- no more delay, no more delay.
Yours is no household fair, no game in a corner --
with you it is fierce sport, roaming the whole world round.
Death is your ferry to the far shore, weeping the wind in your sail --
setting forth, losing yourself -- these play your veena in the soul.
What broke and fell in the dust -- let it go to the flames --
and what has filled, look at that, brother: it wraps the wind, it wraps the sky.
My door stands by the road; I keep it always open.
When will your chariot come -- my eyes keep restless watch.
In Shraban I hear the far clouds set up their deep rumbling,
in Phalgun I hear the rushing wind wake a soft dying murmur --
and in my breast its tremor starts awake, again and again.
I watch everyone go by, never looking back,
singing the road's song in a loud and surging clamor.
The autumn clouds float off, vanishing far away
to some hidden city of music where all roads meet.
To what land, in dream, does my wistful mind-bird fly.
So be it, then -- what has happened to you has happened.
Nothing more came of it -- nothing more, nothing more.
What no one ever cheats you of -- let that much still remain for you;
let the road itself become your home.
Walk straight on, striking the veena's strings,
casting your glance neither right nor left.
Go on losing what lies behind; gather up what you find ahead --
whatever came of it, why should you grieve.
From what forest came the deer that lived in my mind?
Who bound it without cause?
It was the song of moving grace, it was the soul of light and shadow;
it would startle the sky in the forest,
its hooves would sound the yearning of cloudy days
through shade after shade of tamal.
In Phalgun, under the piyal tree, who knew where it fled
with the restlessness of the south wind.
Yours is the beginning, mine is the ending --
you and I together, so the stream flows on.
Your lamp burns, a companion in your house --
for me the night, for me the stars.
You have the shore, I have the water --
yours the sitting still, mine the moving on.
In your hand things keep, in my hand they wear away --
in your heart there is fear, and I am past all fear.
If the days pass like this, then let them pass.
The mind has taken wing -- let it fly, spreading the wings of song.
Today my life's fountain-music has broken loose,
the body's dam has burst --
above my head the deep-blue lid of the sky has come open.
Today the earth has spread out her heart,
as if it were someone's word.
Today the hard earth puts no bar before the mind.
To what tune is it tuned --
the world speaks the heart's own words; let work lie where it falls today.
You would bind me -- do you have the bond that can?
I sue for terms with everyone, to become their captive.
The evening sky bound me without a cord;
night and day the river's unbound current woos me.
The flowers that bloom of themselves, fall of themselves, never stay home --
they are my companions, my friends; they never look behind.
Your vow to catch me is pleaded in vain.
I am bound to myself by the tune of my own song.
One whose heart has swayed of itself, whose mind is lost --
that man is full of fire; caught, can he live?
He, brother, is the wind's comrade, the wave's companion, day and night;
his blood dances only to the rhythm of slipping away.
Again and again you call me in vain, my husband --
the time has come; I shall take my leave.
She whose pyre was decked with insult
has come forth a conqueror of fire.
To the harsh dishonor of a royal throne
she will not yield herself -- she craves freedom.
The earth will take me, her lap outspread,
hidden away from the eyes of all the world;
you stay, and follow a golden Sita.
Over, over at last is this round of trial --
I have passed through the searing blaze of fire.
Mother, O Mother, Mother, O Mother, wake now, Mother --
into your lap I will pour out my basket of insults.
Bring your green anchal, Mother, and lay it upon my body --
loosen from my breast this cruel garland of thorns.
O shackle, I took you on my lap and made you ring.
And you, brother, in joy kept my pride broken.
Playing games with you, my days passed in joy and sorrow --
you ringed my limbs with fetters -- ornaments that cost nothing.
I hold no anger against you; if fault there is, the fault is mine --
if fear stays in my own mind, I see you as fearsome.
Through the whole dark night you were the comrade at my side;
remembering that kindness, I bow to you.
Whoever would seize and bind me, whoever makes this his quest --
will it happen just like that?
He must give himself in bond to lay his bonds on me --
will it happen just like that?
Whoever with sorrow would bring me under his sway --
will it happen just like that?
First his heart of stone must melt into tender pity --
will it happen just like that?
Whoever would make me weep has weeping written in his fate --
will it happen just like that?
I am restless,
I thirst for the far-away.
The days go by; absently I keep watch at the window, hoping for it --
oh, with life and mind I strive to win its touch.
O far-away, vast far-away, you play your yearning flute --
I have no wings, I am bound to one place -- and that I keep forgetting.
I am lost in thought,
O far-away, I am wistful.
In the sun-drenched idle hours, in the murmur of leaves, in the play of shadows,
what form of yours rises glimmering before my eyes in the blue sky.
O far-away, I am wistful.
O far-away, vast far-away, you play your yearning flute --
the door of my chamber is barred -- and that I keep forgetting.
O cautious traveler, for once lose the road and roam.
Blind your two open eyes in a flood of longing tears.
At the end of that forgotten road lies the grove of the lost heart;
heaps of blood-red blossoms lie fallen beneath the thorn tree --
there, morning and evening, the game of breaking and making, on the shore of the shoreless sea.
You sit guarding the hoard of many days;
let it drop away and scatter like flowers on a night of storm.
Come now, wear on your brow the victory-garland of losing everything.
My boat sinks of a sudden
somewhere, on the blow of some stone.
A new boat on its first voyage -- I never set out on fathomless waters --
I sailed her in play, hugging the shoreline.
I floated borne by the current, alone with my hand on the helm --
a sweet mild breeze had touched the sail.
I was content in my own thoughts, not a cloud in the corner of the sky --
in the hope that my boat would land on a bank of flowers.
I have only sown dreams upon the wind --
so I gathered sky-flowers in despair.
Like a shadow the earth melts away; the boat of hope finds no shore;
the mind's idol drifts about the sky.
Nothing was ever caught in this binding of desire alone.
No one was ever captured by mere striving for the far-away.
Sitting alone with my own mind, what games I played with the flame,
and at day's end I see, in anguish, it has all become ash.
Only going and coming, only drifting with the stream,
only weeping and laughing in light and dark.
Only a meeting glimpsed, only a touch in passing,
only a tearful look while drifting far away,
only pressing onward after some new false hope --
leaving vain hopes behind.
Endless longing and broken strength,
desperate labor that reaps a broken harvest,
clinging to a broken boat, adrift on the open sea,
feeling weeps itself away -- in broken words.
Between heart and heart, half an acquaintance,
half a sentence never carried to its end,
in shame, in fear, in dread, in half-belief,
only half a love.
O you there, who will cross to the far shore?
I sit with my boat at the river's edge.
On the far bank, in the groves,
so many games, so many people;
on this bank, empty desert, without water.
While there is still daylight, come -- who will go?
Why waste the hours brooding over this and that?
The sun will go down to its setting,
the fair wind will fall still,
the ferry will cease in the evening dark.
Your gift, this tray of fame, is the last of all my savings --
my heart is afraid to take it.
Once, by night, I came into this world of beauty;
I strung a garland of fallen parijat flowers;
blind in the dark -- it was strung by that very hand --
what does this say of me.
Will you hang it at the throat of Art's own goddess,
where rubies blaze on a seven-strand necklace?
Some day, at heaven's festival,
when the wilted petals loosen and fall,
if this honor then, defeated by shame,
grows dim upon that day.
The dream of a far-off night touches today the smile of the new,
the ache of a far-off Phalgun wakes today in Phalgun's flute.
Alas, that age, alas -- how it slips away
to float in the mirage of this age, in a new enchantment.
The great Time that shed my flowers when my day was done
has set the garland of flowers on your young brow.
Telling me of the ending, it left me weeping in despair,
then in you it filled the emptiness again with new array.
We too played the games, we too have sung the songs.
We too spread our sails, we have rowed our boats.
It is not lost, not lost -- it has not crossed the Baitarani --
in the darting light of young eyes I have found that age again.
O boatman, O boatman of my vessel of human birth,
can you hear from afar the flute of the far shore rising?
Will your boat at day's end come at last to rest at the landing?
Do rows of lamps show themselves there in the evening dark?
It seems to me that on this soft sweet breeze
someone's smile from beyond the sea comes riding the dark today.
At my setting out I gathered and brought along some flowers;
those of them still fresh -- arrange them in the basket while there is time.
Their eyes go running on and on --
down the road of wealth, the road of honor, to the market of beauty, crowd upon crowd.
They have vowed to see, yet the mind knows not whom it would see --
and when they meet the sight of love, their eyes are drowned in their own tears.
Do not call me, all of you --
I will go to the ferry landing, to the sea of formless delight.
A wistful wind fills the sail at the hour of crossing over;
I will go, drowning my two eyes beneath the shoreless sea of nectar.
Krishnakali -- that is what I call her; the village folk call her dark.
On a clouded day I saw in the field the dark cloud's dark deer-eyes.
There was no veil at all upon her head; her loose braid tumbled down her back.
Dark? However dark she may be, I have seen her dark deer-eyes.
Seeing the heavy clouds gather dark, her two dusky cows were lowing;
so the dark girl came hurrying from the hut, anxious, with flurried steps.
Raising her two brows toward the sky, she listened a moment to the rumbling clouds.
Dark? However dark she may be, I have seen her dark deer-eyes.
Suddenly the east wind came racing; a wave ran playing through the paddy field.
I stood alone by the low field-ridge; there was no one else in the field.
Whether or not she looked my way -- I know that, and so does the girl.
Dark? However dark she may be, I have seen her dark deer-eyes.
Just so the dark kohl-black clouds come, in the month of Jyaishtha, to the northeast corner.
Just so the dark soft shadows fall, in the month of Ashadh, on the tamal grove.
Just so, on a Shraban night, a sudden gladness gathers in the heart.
Dark? However dark she may be, I have seen her dark deer-eyes.
Krishnakali -- that is what I call her; let other people say what they will.
In a field in Maynapara I saw the dark girl's dark deer-eyes.
She had not drawn her cloth up over her head; she had no time to feel her shame.
Dark? However dark she may be, I have seen her dark deer-eyes.
